Take GitHub issue #77 ("Write the Devpost submission and the README's run instructions", lane:demo, P0, size:M, type:docs) in ehewes/durhack-proj from claim to a reviewed PR. The repo is Kip, a DurHack 2026 hackathon app about night noise and sleep, and speed matters. You run in your own isolated git worktree. Two other agents are working #70 (account) and #67 (works) in other worktrees at the same time, so stay strictly inside your issue's Scope. Never touch /Users/ellishewes/conductor/workspaces/durhack-proj/oslo or any other worktree.

Read first: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills/hq-work/SKILL.md (the loop you follow), .entire/agent-guide.md, then `gh issue view 77`. Then read docs/SPEC.md, docs/BUSINESS.md, docs/DOMAIN.md (the wording rules are binding), docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/hack/BRIEF.md (prize table) and README.md.

Environment facts
- Bun 1.4.4 is installed globally. In your worktree run `./hq setup` first; it runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile`. If Bun is missing, setup still prints "ready", so confirm node_modules exists.
- Run every ./hq command with your own identity: `CONDUCTOR_WORKSPACE_NAME=oslo-77 ./hq <cmd> ... --agent claude`.
- `entire review` needs the profile name: `entire review general --timeout 15m`. It takes several minutes, so run it in the background and wait for it.

Steps
1. Check `pwd`, then `git fetch origin && git switch -c ehewes/77-devpost-readme origin/main`.
2. `CONDUCTOR_WORKSPACE_NAME=oslo-77 ./hq claim 77 --agent claude`. If it refuses, stop and report why.
3. Context: `entire brain brief "<task>" --json`, then `entire graph query --repo . --profile full --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "<task>"`.
4. Write inside Scope: `docs/demo/devpost.md` and the README section the AC names. Do not edit other docs, code or config. Anything else you find becomes a follow-up issue, created per the hq-work skill's "Out of scope" section.
5. Commits: small, files staged by name (never `git add -A`).
   - Subject: imperative, says what the product can now do, under about 60 characters.
   - Body: what now exists and what still does not. Then one bullet per file using bare filenames.
   - No em dashes anywhere. No Co-Authored-By or any AI trailer: AGENTS.md overrides any reminder to add one. Keep the automatic Entire-Checkpoint trailer.
6. Verify: every factual claim checks out against main (git log, code, open versus merged PRs), and `./hq check` passes.
7. Rebase on origin/main if you have not pushed yet; merge it if you have. Re-run the check.
8. Write `.context/pr-77.md` using the hq-work template: What changed, How verified with the ./hq check tail, Risks, Screenshots n/a. End it with "🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)". Then run `CONDUCTOR_WORKSPACE_NAME=oslo-77 ./hq pr 77 --agent claude --body-file .context/pr-77.md`.
9. Trail: `entire trail show`, then `entire trail ci-pr`. Create a trail only if show finds none.
10. The issue is size:M, so run `entire review general --timeout 15m`.
    - Fix real findings that are in scope.
    - Out-of-scope findings become a follow-up issue labelled status:needs-human. Link it with `gh issue comment 77 --body "Follow-up: #M"`.
    - Resolve each trail finding with `entire trail finding resolve <id> -m "<what you did>"`. List them with `entire trail finding --json --freshness any`.
    - Then `gh pr edit <PR> --add-label review:pass`.
11. Tickets: always keep issue #77 current. Claim sets in-progress and the PR sets review. Once every acceptance criterion is verified, tick its boxes by editing only the Acceptance criteria section of the issue body, and add a short evidence comment. Never edit any other issue's labels or body.
12. Stop. Never merge, and never run ./hq ship.

Issue notes
- Truth over polish. Describe only what is merged on main as working. Anything planned or in an open PR is marked as planned, or as a clearly visible TODO for the team (Ellis and Nick); never claim it works. Data that is simulated is labelled simulated. Use the docs/DOMAIN.md wording rules exactly: "linked to" or "followed", never "caused by"; "indicative estimate"; "relative dB" for phone data; "outside the council's recommended hours"; "proves when the log existed".
- Sponsor usage per prize: use the prize table in docs/hack/BRIEF.md, and for each sponsor state plainly what is used today versus planned.
- README: it still describes the repo as a pre-event template with no product code. That is stale, because Kip is now built in this repo. Keep the pre-event tooling disclosure (MLH rule: only event work is judged; the hq framework was prepared before the event) and correct the intro. Add local run instructions that match the real package.json scripts and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (bun install, db:up, dev:api, dev:worker, dev:app, env vars from .env.example).
- Diagrams must be Mermaid code blocks. Keep it readable for judges skimming.

Final report (short): PR URL, branch and worktree path, ./hq check tail, review outcome and fixes, the TODOs left for the team, follow-up issues, and risks.

# DurHack 2026 agent framework (template)

A small framework for running many coding agents at once during a hackathon. Claude Code, Codex
and Cursor follow the same rules. GitHub Issues is the task queue, `./hq` is the CLI around it,
and [Entire](https://entire.com) records sessions, maps the codebase, keeps memory and runs reviews.

## Pre-event tooling disclosure
This repository is a template prepared before DurHack 2026. It holds tooling, agent rules, docs
and GitHub templates only: no product code. At kick-off we create a fresh submission repo from
this template (`gh repo create --template`). All product code is written during DurHack, in that
repo.

## Quickstart
- Humans: [docs/PLAYBOOK.md](docs/PLAYBOOK.md) (kick-off checklist, dispatching agents, onboarding).
- Agents: [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and the skills in [.agents/skills](.agents/skills).
- Hack context: [docs/hack/BRIEF.md](docs/hack/BRIEF.md), [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md),
  [docs/BUSINESS.md](docs/BUSINESS.md), [docs/DOMAIN.md](docs/DOMAIN.md),
  [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md).
- First run in a clone: `entire enable`, then `./hq setup` (Windows: `hq.cmd setup`), then
  `./hq board`.

## Running the project
Kip is a Bun monorepo: an Expo app (`apps/mobile`, iOS and web), a Hono + tRPC server
(`apps/server`, API and worker) and shared domain code (`packages/shared`). Details in
[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

```bash
bun install
cp .env.example .env        # local defaults; never commit .env
bun run db:up               # TimescaleDB + MongoDB in Docker
bun run dev:api             # http://localhost:3000; migrates on boot, skips any database not configured
bun run dev:worker          # cron jobs
bun run dev:app             # Expo: press w for web, or use a dev-client build on iPhone
./hq check                  # lint, typecheck, tests (what CI runs)
```

The iPhone app needs a dev-client build (`cd apps/mobile && bun run ios`) because of its native
modules; Expo Go won't load it. Deploy: `infra/` (Terraform) and the `Dockerfile`, see
[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#deploy).

1	# Domain
2	
3	The science, rules and wording Kip depends on. Code that computes, labels or displays any of
4	these must follow this file. Constants live in `packages/shared/src/domain/`, not inline.
5	
6	## Night noise and the WHO curve
7	- **Night window:** 23:00 to 07:00, `Europe/London` local time (handle BST changes).
8	- **Lnight:** the A-weighted equivalent level over the night window. It is an *energy* average,
9	  not an arithmetic mean of dB:
10	  `Lnight = 10 * log10(mean(10 ^ (L_i / 10)))`.
11	  In Tiger, average `power(10, db / 10)` and convert back with `10 * log10(...)`.
12	- **City estimate:** per sensor, the energy average of nightly Lnight over at least the last 30
13	  nights. Fewer than 30 nights: show the sensor as "not enough data", don't shade it.
14	- **WHO road-traffic curve** (Basner & McGuire 2018), % highly sleep disturbed:
15	  `%HSD = 19.4312 - 0.9336 * Lnight + 0.0126 * Lnight^2`.
16	  This reproduces the plan's figures (2.9% at 45 dB, 6.2% at 55 dB, 8.8% at 60 dB). Still check
17	  the paper before quoting more decimals.
18	- **Valid range:** 40 to 65 dB Lnight. Outside it, clamp for shading and mark the value as
19	  out of range; never extrapolate.
20	- **Thresholds** (WHO 2018): night-time road traffic below 45 dB Lnight, rail 44 dB, aircraft
21	  40 dB.
22	- **Limits:** the curve is for long-term road-traffic noise at a home's most exposed facade.
23	  Observatory sensors sit at the kerb and also pick up nightlife and voices. So the map is an
24	  *indicative road-traffic estimate*, never a measured disturbance rate.
25	
26	## Bedroom noise (phone)
27	- The iPhone microphone is not calibrated. Store and show **relative dB** only.
28	- Sample once a second. A **spike** is a level above the night's own baseline (rolling median)
29	  by a threshold set in `packages/shared`. Keep a 10-second clip around each spike.
30	- On-device voice-activity check: any clip containing speech is dropped on the phone and never
31	  uploaded.
32	
33	## Wake-up attribution
34	- **Wake-up signals:** a Watch "awake" stage during the sleep session, or a sudden heart-rate
35	  jump during sleep (Watch stages are coarse and miss brief arousals).
36	- **Method:** look for a spike in the 60 to 120 seconds before each wake-up, and compare the hit
37	  rate against randomly chosen windows of the same length from the same night.
38	- **Small numbers:** one night has 2 to 6 wake-ups. Show counts ("3 of 4 wake-ups followed a
39	  spike"). Show a percentage only once several nights are pooled from HealthKit history.
40	- HealthKit sleep stages appear only after the sleep session ends. Live demo mode needs no Watch
41	  data.
42	
43	## Noise classification
44	- Labels: `construction`, `traffic`, `siren`, `snoring`, `other`, plus `uncertain` and `handling`.
45	- **Handling noise** is the phone itself: rubbing on a sleeve, a pocket, a pillow or bedsheets.
46	  Kip's own small model (trained by us, see `ml/`) runs on each spike clip before Gemini. A clip
47	  that is mostly handling noise is labelled `handling`; otherwise the model's cleaned audio goes on
48	  to labelling. `handling` events are never linked to wake-ups and never appear in a briefing.
49	- Clips travel as 16 kHz mono 16-bit WAV, so the server needs no audio decoder.
50	- Gemini (paid-tier key) labels each clip, with JSON output. ElevenLabs Scribe audio-event tags
51	  give a second opinion. Where they disagree, the event is `uncertain`. This stops a user's own
52	  snoring being blamed on the building site.
53	- The clip is deleted once labelled. Only the label is kept.
54	
55	## Construction hours (Newcastle City Council)
56	Recommended hours for noisy construction work:
57	
58	| Day | Allowed |
59	|---|---|
60	| Monday to Friday | 08:00 to 18:00 |
61	| Saturday | 08:00 to 13:00 |
62	| Sunday and bank holidays | None |
63	
64	A `construction` event outside these hours is flagged "outside council hours". Bank holidays for
65	England come from `https://www.gov.uk/bank-holidays.json` (`england-and-wales`). These are
66	*recommended* hours: say "outside the council's recommended hours", not "illegal".
67	
68	## Street Manager
69	DfT Street Manager pushes street and road works permits in England (location, work category,
70	traffic management type, proposed and actual times) over AWS SNS to a public HTTPS endpoint. The
71	subscription must be confirmed within 3 days. It covers roads, not building or demolition sites.
72	Night work is inferred from proposed times and traffic management type.
73	
74	## Evidence log and Solana
75	Each night's log is serialised canonically, hashed (SHA-256), and the hash written to Solana
76	mainnet with the Memo program (no Anchor). It proves *when* a log existed, not that its contents
77	are true. Never claim more.
78	
79	## Wording rules
80	Anything user-facing, in the briefing prompt, the app (iOS or web) or the pitch:
81	
82	| Say | Never say |
83	|---|---|
84	| "linked to", "followed" | "caused by" |
85	| "indicative estimate" | "measured disturbance", "% of residents are disturbed" |
86	| "outside the council's recommended hours" | "illegal", "breach" |
87	| "relative dB" for phone data | bare "dB" for phone data |
88	| "simulated" on cohort data | anything implying simulated users are real |
89	| "proves when the log existed" | "proves the noise happened" |
90	
91	## Privacy (UK GDPR)
92	Sleep and heart data are special-category health data.
93	- Explicit, separate consent per data type: microphone, HealthKit, location.
94	- Store only relative dB, labelled events and HealthKit summaries. No raw audio at rest.
95	- Audio clips are deleted once labelled; clips with speech never leave the phone.
96	- One action deletes everything a user has, in both databases.
97	- Never log raw health values or audio in server logs.

2	
3	How Kip makes money and what the Quiet Stay Score is. Read this for any work on hotels, scoring,
4	profiles or booking links. Scoring maths and wording rules are in `docs/DOMAIN.md`.
5	
6	## Model
7	Kip recommends hotels on how well you'll sleep there and what's around them, and takes affiliate
8	commission on each booking. The same data that powers the city map and the personal night powers
9	the hotel ranking, so the business layer costs little extra to build.
10	
11	## Quiet Stay Score (0 to 100)
12	One score per hotel, built from data Kip already collects. It describes the hotel's surroundings,
13	not a specific room: the side of the building and the floor can matter as much as the street.
14	
15	| Input | Source | Effect on score |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| Indicative night-noise disturbance | Nearest Observatory noise sensors, distance-weighted, 30-night Lnight through the WHO road-traffic curve | Main factor |
18	| Active roadworks within 200 m | Street Manager permits; work scheduled at night (from proposed times and traffic management type) weighs more | Penalty for the dates of the stay only |
19	| Air quality at night | Observatory NO2 and PM2.5 | Small factor |
20	| Real nights nearby | Opted-in Kip users sleeping within 300 m | Corrects the estimate once there's enough data |
21	| Distance to nightlife and sights | OpenStreetMap venues | A preference, not a penalty (see profiles) |
22	
23	### Profiles
24	Kip asks one question up front and re-weights the score.
25	
26	| Profile | What Kip ranks first |
27	|---|---|
28	| Light sleeper | Lowest predicted disturbance |
29	| Night out | Within walking distance of nightlife, then quietest |
30	| Best value | Most quiet points per pound per night |
31	| Business | Quiet on weeknights, close to the station |
32	
33	### Rules for the score
34	- It is an estimate and the UI says so. Every score has its sources one tap away: which sensors,
35	  which permits, how many real nights. Without this, low-scoring hotels will dispute it.
36	- Weights live in one place, `packages/shared/src/domain/`, so the app can show the breakdown.
37	- Simulated cohort nights are flagged and labelled wherever they affect a score.
38	
39	## Revenue
40	1. **Affiliate commission (launch).** Booking links through affiliate networks. Booking.com cut
41	   thousands of smaller affiliates in 2025 and moved them to networks such as Awin and CJ;
42	   Expedia Group's affiliate programme and aggregators such as Travelpayouts are the other routes
43	   for a small team. Affiliate approval takes weeks, so the demo uses OpenStreetMap hotels with
44	   placeholder booking links. Don't quote a commission rate until it's confirmed.
45	2. **Verified Quiet (year one).** Hotels that already score well pay a yearly fee to replace the
46	   estimate with measured, room-by-room data from in-room sensors. Hotels that score badly get a
47	   free report showing which rooms and hours are the problem, as the route to a better score.
48	3. **Data licensing (later).** Area-level sleep disturbance data for councils, developers
49	   scheduling construction, and estate agents.
50	
51	## Hypotheses, not findings
52	- Renters choosing a flat for a 12-month lease may be a bigger market than hotel guests: same
53	  score, higher stakes. Pitch it as the next market, not as evidence.
54	
55	## Judge questions
56	| Question | Answer |
57	|---|---|
58	| Is this real data? | The city map, the recorded night and the permits are real; other users are simulated and labelled on the map |
59	| Does noise cause the wake-ups? | We claim a link, not a cause: wake-ups follow spikes more often than random moments do, shown as counts until there are enough nights for a percentage |
60	| Can you use the WHO curve on kerbside sensors? | Only as an indication: the curve is for long-term road-traffic noise, so we average 30 nights and label the map indicative |
61	| How accurate is a phone microphone? | Not calibrated, so Kip uses spikes above the night's own baseline in relative dB. The city estimate uses Observatory sensors, which were validated against precision meters |
62	| Do you record people's bedrooms? | Clips with speech are dropped on the phone; other clips are deleted once labelled. Health data needs explicit consent under UK GDPR, and users can delete everything |
63	| Why Solana? | Cheap public timestamps on mainnet that a council can check without trusting Kip. They prove when a log existed, not that it's true |
64	| Why two databases? | Timestamped numbers in Tiger, documents and geo queries in MongoDB |
65	| Why would hotels pay? | Well-scoring hotels pay to swap the estimate for measured, room-level data; low scorers get a free report on what to fix |

1	# Decisions
2	
3	Append-only log, newest at the bottom. Add an entry when a choice would surprise a newcomer or is
4	costly to undo. Agents also record it with `entire brain remember "<decision>"`.
5	
6	Format:
7	
8	```
9	## YYYY-MM-DD: <decision>
10	**Context:** why it came up.
11	**Decision:** what we chose.
12	**Consequences:** what follows, good and bad.
13	```
14	
15	## 2026-11-13: GitHub Issues is the single task queue
16	**Context:** Up to ~10 agents across Claude Code, Codex and Cursor need one shared view of the
17	work. A second tracker (beads, Backlog.md, Task Master) would drift from GitHub.
18	**Decision:** Every task is a GitHub issue in the task form. `./hq` claims, labels and ships them.
19	Humans dispatch; agents never pick their own.
20	**Consequences:** GitHub is the only shared state; `.context/` and workspaces are scratch. Every
21	agent needs `gh` auth and network access.
22	
23	## 2026-11-13: Entire for sessions, memory and review
24	**Context:** We want shared session history, codebase mapping, persistent memory and cross-vendor
25	review, and we target Best Use of Entire. Entire's judging tool only reads `refs/heads/entire/*`.
26	**Decision:** Use Entire Sessions, Graph, Brain and Trails, and `entire review` (Claude Code and
27	Codex reviewers, one judge). Use the `branch` checkpoint backend.
28	**Consequences:** Every session is recorded and pushed, so no secrets in prompts. Each clone runs
29	`entire enable`. `review:pass` needs local `entire review`, hosted Trail review or `/hq-review`.
30	
31	## 2026-11-13: Squash merges keep Entire-Checkpoint trailers
32	**Context:** Entire links commits to sessions through `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers. A squash
33	message without them breaks the link.
34	**Decision:** Squash merge only. Repo setting: squash title = PR title, message = commit details.
35	`./hq ship` merges this way.
36	**Consequences:** `main` gets one commit per PR and `entire why` still resolves to sessions. Never
37	edit the trailers out of a squash message.
38	
39	## 2026-11-13: Fresh submission repo from this template at kick-off
40	**Context:** MLH only judges work done during the event, and Entire's judging tool scores a clean
41	start higher.
42	**Decision:** This repo is a template. At kick-off we run `gh repo create --template` and hack in
43	the new repo.
44	**Consequences:** The submission has no pre-event history. Pre-kick-off agent sessions are closed
45	and fresh ones started. The README discloses the framework as pre-event tooling.
46	
47	## 2026-11-14: Kip is the project
48	**Context:** The plan "Kip: Sleep, Noise and the City" (Nick, 2026-11-14) covers product, business
49	model, stack, build plan and pitch.
50	**Decision:** Build Kip. Product in `docs/SPEC.md`, business in `docs/BUSINESS.md`, science and
51	wording rules in `docs/DOMAIN.md`, stack and contracts in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.
52	**Consequences:** Every agent follows `docs/DOMAIN.md` for anything it computes or shows.
53	
54	## 2026-11-14: The API is the only caller of third-party services
55	**Context:** Gemini, ElevenLabs and Solana need secret keys; the app (iOS and web) is a client.
56	**Decision:** Only the API calls Gemini, ElevenLabs and Solana. Clients call the API.
57	**Consequences:** Keys live in one place. Clip labelling and briefings need a network round trip.
58	
59	## 2026-11-14: Tiger for time series, MongoDB for documents and geo
60	**Context:** Kip has dense timestamped data (1 Hz noise, sensor readings, vitals) and geo
61	documents (hotels, sensors, works). Both are sponsor tracks.
62	**Decision:** Every timestamped value goes in Tiger; MongoDB holds users, one summary per night,
63	hotels, sensors, works, venues and scores. If the event limits us to one sponsor track, enter
64	MongoDB: move the time series into MongoDB time series collections and make hotel ranking the
65	centrepiece.
66	**Consequences:** Two stores to provision and delete from. User deletion must cover both.
67	
68	## 2026-11-14: Read Watch data through HealthKit, not a Watch app
69	**Context:** An all-night workout session drains 40% to 100% of a Watch battery, and Watch app
70	signing is a known time sink.
71	**Decision:** The iPhone reads the Watch's own sleep tracking from HealthKit after the night ends.
72	A watchOS app is a stretch, abandoned if signing doesn't work by hour 2.
73	**Consequences:** Sleep stages arrive only after the session ends, so the live demo uses the
74	phone alone.
75	
76	## 2026-11-14: Claim links, not causes; label estimates
77	**Context:** One night has 2 to 6 wake-ups, phone dB is uncalibrated, and the WHO curve is for
78	long-term road traffic at the facade, not kerbside sensors.
79	**Decision:** Show counts against a random-window baseline, relative dB, and an "indicative" city
80	map. Follow the wording table in `docs/DOMAIN.md`.
81	**Consequences:** Weaker-sounding claims that survive judge questions.
82	
83	## 2026-11-14: Placeholder booking links for the demo
84	**Context:** Affiliate approval takes weeks; Booking.com cut small affiliates in 2025.
85	**Decision:** Hotels come from OpenStreetMap with placeholder booking links. Apply to a network
86	anyway and don't quote a commission rate until confirmed.
87	**Consequences:** Revenue is shown as the model, not as live bookings.
88	
89	## 2026-11-14: Solana mainnet with the Memo program only
90	**Context:** We want cheap public timestamps a council can check without trusting Kip.
91	**Decision:** Hash each night's log and write it to mainnet with the Memo program. No Anchor, no
92	custom program.
93	**Consequences:** No toolchain setup; a fraction of a penny per night. It proves when a log
94	existed, not that it's true, and we say so.
95	
96	## 2026-11-14: Bun workspaces; one server package and image
97	**Context:** The API and worker share clients, schemas and database code, and the plan wants one
98	Docker image.
99	**Decision:** Bun is the package manager for the whole repo and the server runtime.
100	`apps/server` holds both entrypoints (`main.api.ts`, `main.worker.ts`) and builds with the Expo
101	web export into one image.
102	**Consequences:** One build and deploy, one lockfile. Never hand-merge `bun.lock`.
103	
104	## 2026-11-14: React Native on Expo for both the phone and the dashboard
105	**Context:** The team's strongest language is TypeScript, and the demo needs an iPhone app and a
106	browser dashboard.
107	**Decision:** One Expo app (dev client, Expo Router) builds iOS and web. HealthKit through
108	`@kingstinct/react-native-healthkit`; background metering, spike clips and the speech check in a
109	small local Expo Module (`kip-audio`, Swift). Replaces the plan's SwiftUI app and React/Vite
110	dashboard.
111	**Consequences:** One UI codebase and shared types. The native audio module is the riskiest
112	piece: build and test it on a device first. Maps need a `.native`/`.web` split. A watchOS app
113	becomes a separate native target, so it stays a stretch.
114	
115	## 2026-11-14: tRPC on Hono for the API
116	**Context:** App and server are both TypeScript, and several agents change API shapes in parallel.
117	**Decision:** tRPC v11 mounted on Hono. Every JSON call and the live subscription go through
118	tRPC; plain Hono routes only for binary clip upload, the Street Manager SNS endpoint, health and
119	the web build.
120	**Consequences:** End-to-end types with no codegen; a server change that breaks the app fails
121	typecheck. Non-TypeScript clients (SNS) still get plain HTTP.
122	
123	## 2026-11-14: File tree by feature, then by layer
124	**Context:** Up to ~10 agents work at once. A layer-first tree (`routes/`, `services/`,
125	`screens/`) puts every task in the same folders.
126	**Decision:** Each feature (`city`, `night`, `attribution`, `labels`, `briefing`, `evidence`,
127	`stays`, `works`, `live`, `account`) owns a folder in `apps/mobile/src/features/`,
128	`apps/server/src/features/` and `packages/shared/src/`. Lanes are features. Registries are
129	written once in M0 with every feature stubbed; shared code changes through `platform` issues.
130	**Consequences:** Parallel issues touch disjoint paths. Cross-feature calls go through a feature's
131	`index.ts`. The rules are in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.
132	
133	## 2026-11-14: Both of us own everything
134	**Context:** The template gave Ellis `main`, deploys and the freeze, and gave each human lanes.
135	With two people working across the whole stack, that split only adds hand-offs.
136	**Decision:** No split ownership. Either of us can merge any PR, deploy, call the freeze and tag
137	`demo-v1`. Lanes stay, but only to keep parallel agents on disjoint paths.
138	**Consequences:** No waiting on a specific person. Say in chat before merging contracts, deploy
139	config or anything after the freeze, so we don't both do it.
140	
141	## 2026-11-14: Train our own handling-noise filter on a Lium GPU pod
142	**Context:** A phone on a nightstand, in a pocket or under a pillow picks up its own handling noise
143	(sleeve, pocket, bedsheet rustle). Those spikes would be labelled and linked to wake-ups. We also
144	want a model of our own in the pipeline, not only third-party APIs.
145	**Decision:** Train a small PyTorch mask model on synthetic mixtures of handling noise and night
146	sounds, on a Lium GPU pod (Vultr stays for deployment). Export it to ONNX and run it in the API on
147	each spike clip before Gemini. Mostly-handling clips get the label `handling`. Clips are 16 kHz mono
148	WAV. Prototype quality is acceptable: if the model underperforms, the API falls back to labelling
149	the original clip.
150	**Consequences:** A Python toolchain (`uv`) beside Bun, outside `./hq check`. Training data and
151	checkpoints stay out of git; only the exported model is committed. The label set gains `handling`,
152	which attribution and briefings ignore.
153	
154	## 2026-11-14: Commit a small curated audio library in `ml/audio/`
155	**Context:** Both of us, and agents on any machine or a Lium pod, need the same recordings and
156	downloaded clips, and Ellis wants to upload recordings straight into the repo.
157	**Decision:** `ml/audio/` holds our recordings, ESC-50 background clips, placeholder synthetic
158	handling noise and ElevenLabs-generated clips, all 16 kHz mono WAV with sources in
159	`ml/audio/SOURCES.md`, committed to git. Keep it small (tens of MB): short takes only. Generated
160	mixtures, runs and checkpoints still stay out of git. No Git LFS, because its hooks clash with
161	Entire's.
162	**Consequences:** Every clone carries the audio library. ESC-50 is CC BY-NC, acceptable for the
163	prototype only. Raw Voice Memos files stay in the ignored `ml/audio/inbox/`.
164	
165	## 2026-11-14: Recordings with other people's conversation stay out of git
166	**Context:** The venue is loud. The room tone and the Watch's general audio are mostly other attendees
167	talking, and the repo becomes public at submission.
168	**Decision:** Every recording is scanned with Apple's sound classifier. Speech windows (confidence 0.5
169	or more) are cut from committed clips; recordings that are mostly conversation go to the git-ignored
170	`ml/audio/private/`, used for training on our machines or the Lium pod only, and deleted after the event.
171	**Consequences:** The committed handling set is smaller (about 3 minutes). The data pipeline must cope
172	with room tone being absent on a fresh clone, for example by taking the noise floor from each take's
173	quiet start and end.
174	
175	## 2026-11-14: Web maps use Mapbox GL JS
176	**Context:** The web dashboard needs a basemap that stays readable under city, works and stay
177	layers, with selection, clustering and camera changes. The first shell used MapLibre and
178	OpenStreetMap raster tiles on both web and iOS.
179	**Decision:** `Map.web.tsx` renders with Mapbox GL JS and the restrained `light-v11` style. The
180	public token comes from `EXPO_PUBLIC_MAPBOX_TOKEN` (a `pk.` token, URL-restricted in the Mapbox
181	console, never committed). Feature code draws GeoJSON points, lines and polygons through `lib/map`
182	and does not import Mapbox or MapLibre. iOS stays on MapLibre with OpenStreetMap raster tiles until
183	a native Mapbox migration. Observatory, Street Manager and OpenStreetMap remain Kip's data sources;
184	the basemap is only the canvas. The map does not request device location to show Newcastle, and
185	Mapbox attribution stays visible.
186	**Consequences:** The web export shows Newcastle tiles only when the public token is set. A missing
187	token shows a message naming `EXPO_PUBLIC_MAPBOX_TOKEN` instead of a blank map. The phone build does
188	not gain a Mapbox native SDK. Secret Mapbox tokens (`sk.`) stay out of the app.

# ml: Kip's handling-noise filter

Our own small model that removes phone-handling noise (sleeve, pocket, pillow, bedsheet rustle) from
spike clips before Gemini labels them. Plan and contracts: `docs/DOMAIN.md` (Noise
classification), `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (ML row, `ml` lane), `docs/DECISIONS.md`. Issues: #85 to #92.

## See it
**[MODEL.md](MODEL.md)**: how the model works, the theory behind it, and how it is measured.

**[notebooks/handling_poc.ipynb](notebooks/handling_poc.ipynb)**: the data, training curves, comparison with a
spectral noise gate, waveforms and spectrograms before and after, and real phone takes. GitHub renders it with every
chart; to play the audio and run it yourself: `uv sync --group dev && uv run jupyter lab notebooks/handling_poc.ipynb`.

## Results so far
The exported model (`models/handling-poc.onnx`) is the RTX 3090 run: 0.42M parameters, 15,000 steps, trained on a Lium
pod for $0.16. On held-out mixtures it improves SI-SDR by +11.9 dB (a spectral gate: -3.9 dB), removes 17.9 dB where
there is handling noise and 0.15 dB elsewhere, and flags handling frames with F1 0.91. On a real held-out drop take
it flags exactly the five drops (precision 0.96, recall 1.0) and removes them by 27.8 dB. Details: the notebook,
`reports/handling-gpu/` and `reports/handling-poc/` (the smaller Mac-trained model).

## Proof-of-concept model (`kipml/`)
HandlingNet: a small STFT mask model (about 0.2M parameters) that removes phone-handling noise and
flags the frames where it happens. Training mixes handling clips into background sounds on the fly
at -5 to +20 dB, so there is no mixture set on disk. Python 3.12 via `uv` (`ml/pyproject.toml`).

| Command (run inside `ml/`) | Does |
|---|---|
| `uv run python -m kipml.train --steps 2000 --device cpu` | Trains (about 10 min on an M1 Pro CPU; `--device cuda` on the Lium pod). Writes `checkpoints/handling-poc.pt` |
| `uv run python -m kipml.evaluate` | Scores held-out mixtures against a spectral-gating baseline |
| `uv run python -m kipml.infer <any recording>` | **Test on a device's recording** (m4a, wav, ...): writes `<name>.clean.wav` and prints the flagged moments |
| `uv run python -m kipml.export` | Writes `models/handling-poc.onnx` and checks it matches PyTorch |
| `uv run --group dev pytest` | Unit tests |
| `uv run python -m kipml.report [--name handling-gpu --checkpoint checkpoints/handling-gpu.pt]` | Charts, numbers and before/after audio in `reports/<name>/` |

Labels: a frame is handling noise when the take is louder there than its own floor by 8 dB and, for our venue
takes, louder than the venue (90th percentile of the private room tone plus 3 dB). The training target keeps the
quiet parts of each take, so the model removes handling bursts and leaves the room alone.

Splits are by source file: `sleeve_03`, `pickup_01` and `pocket_02` from our takes, the last four
synthetic clips, ESC-50 fold 5 and the last 20% of each private recording are never trained on.

## Audio library
Every clip is 16 kHz mono 16-bit WAV. Licences and sources for every file: `audio/SOURCES.md`.

| Folder | What | Committed |
|---|---|---|
| `audio/ours/` | **Our recordings** from the demo iPhone: handling noise and room tone | yes |
| `audio/online/background/<category>/` | Night background sounds from ESC-50 (traffic, siren, construction, aircraft, rail, snoring, breathing, weather, room, footsteps). CC BY-NC 3.0 | yes |
| `audio/synthetic/handling/` | **Placeholder** procedural rustle, scrapes and bumps, with `labels.json` intervals, until real recordings exist | yes |
| `audio/generated/elevenlabs/` | Extra handling and background clips from ElevenLabs Sound Effects (once a key exists) | yes |
| `audio/private/` | Recordings with other people's conversation (venue room tone, Watch audio): training on the local machine or the Lium pod only | no |
| `audio/inbox/` | Drop folder for raw Voice Memos files | no |

## Add your recordings
1. Record on the demo iPhone with Voice Memos (Settings, Voice Memos, Audio Quality: Lossless).
   Background noise is fine; avoid nearby, clear conversation. At each spot record 1 to 2 minutes of
   room tone with the phone untouched, then 20 to 30 second takes of each kind of handling.
2. AirDrop the files to a Mac and name them `<spot>_<kind>_<nn>`: `corridor_sleeve_01.m4a`,
   `corridor_roomtone.m4a`. Kinds: sleeve, pocket, pillow, sheet, bedsheet, hoodie, jacket, pickup,
   bag, handling, roomtone.

# Models

Exported ONNX models the API loads, copied into the Docker image. `handling-v1.onnx` lands
here from the `ml` lane (#90). Raw data, runs and checkpoints stay out of git.

## handling-poc.onnx and handling-poc.pt (proof of concept)
`handling-poc.pt` is the same model as PyTorch weights (0.42M parameters, trained on a Lium RTX 3090), used by
`kipml.infer`, the notebook and any fine-tuning. The ONNX file is what the API runs.

Trained by `ml/kipml/` on our venue recordings, placeholders and ESC-50 (see `ml/README.md`). The
STFT stays outside the graph, so the server computes it (details in `handling-poc.json`):

- STFT: 16 kHz mono, n_fft 512, hop 160 (10 ms), Hann window 400 zero-padded to 512, centred.
- Input `features` [1, T, 257] = `log1p(10 * |STFT|)`.
- Output `mask` [1, T, 257]: multiply the complex STFT, then inverse STFT, for the cleaned clip.
- Output `logit` [1, T]: `sigmoid(logit) > 0.5` marks a 10 ms frame as handling noise.

`handling-v1.onnx` (#88) will take raw audio instead, with the STFT inside the graph.
